summary: This note covers Avicenna (Ibn Sina, born c. 980 near Bukhara), the Persian polymath of the Islamic Golden Age. It discusses debates over his religious affiliation, his early education, his metaphysics of essence and existence, and his influence on medicine, astronomy, theology and psychology. It ends with his legacy in modern Iran and in institutions and places named after him.
one_line: Overview of Avicenna's life, scholarly debates about his faith, his philosophy, medicine, astronomy and psychology, and his lasting legacy.
key_facts: Avicenna was born c. 980 in Afšana, a village near Bukhara, the capital of the Samanids, a Persian dynasty in Central Asia and Greater Khorasan.
His mother Setareh was from Bukhara; his father Abdullah was a respected Ismaili scholar from Balkh, though this is not universally agreed upon.
According to his autobiography, Avicenna had memorised the entire Quran by the age of 10.
He studied Fiqh under the Sunni Hanafi scholar Ismail al-Zahid and learned Indian arithmetic from an Indian greengrocer, Mahmoud Massahi.
Dimitri Gutas, Aisha Khan and Jules J. Janssens demonstrated that Avicenna was a Sunni Hanafi, while Ẓahīr al-dīn al-Bayhaqī (d. 1169) considered him a follower of the Brethren of Purity.
Following al-Farabi, Avicenna distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud), arguing that existence must be due to an agent-cause that gives existence to an essence.
George Sarton called Ibn Sīnā "one of the greatest thinkers and medical scholars in history".

His Canon of Medicine linked Galen's medical writings with Aristotle's philosophy, and from the early fourteenth to the mid-sixteenth centuries he was ranked with Hippocrates and Galen as princeps medicorum ("prince of physicians").

Avicenna claimed to have observed Venus as a spot on the Sun, possibly the transit of May 24, 1032, though modern scholars suspect he mistook a sunspot; he argued that stars and planets are self-luminous.
His "flying man" argument in the Psychology of The Cure I.1.7 defends the soul as without quantitative extension and has an affinity with Descartes's cogito.
His Kitab al-nafs parts of Kitab al-shifa (The Book of Healing) and Kitab al-najat (The Book of Deliverance) were known in Latin as De Anima.
His theological views formed part of the core curriculum at Islamic religious schools until the 19th century.
The Avicenna Mausoleum and Museum in Hamadan was built in 1952, and a crater on the Moon and the plant genus Avicennia are named after him.
Before leaving Khwarezm, Avicenna met Al-Biruni, Abu Nasr Iraqi, Abu Sahl Masihi and Abu al-Khayr Khammar, according to Aruzi Samarqandi.
